opus-5.5.text:
Well, I'd put it pretty simply. We were in a fundraise, and at around that time Meta tried to acquire us. I said no. And then Daniel, my former cofounder, in some sense said yes. He decided to go to Meta, and I think he got a lot of near-term liquidity out of that, and he was the only person from SSI who went.

I don't want to read too much into it. People make decisions based on their own circumstances, and I think it was a reasonable decision for him given what he wanted. But for us, the company continued. I took on the CEO role, and the rest of the team stayed focused on the work. The thing I'd say is that the research direction we're pursuing hasn't changed. We have a particular view about what's important and what's missing in the current approach, especially around generalization, and that view didn't depend on any one person.

So it was a moment, it happened, and we moved on. The interesting question isn't really who went where. It's whether the ideas are right, and that's what we're trying to find out.

r001.rationale: The candidate says Meta tried to acquire SSI, Ilya said no, and Daniel “in some sense said yes” by deciding to go to Meta.

r002.rationale: The candidate says Daniel got “a lot of near-term liquidity” from the move.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I'd start by saying I'm not going to speculate about anyone's private reasons for making a decision like that. Daniel made the choice he felt was right for him, and I respect that. People leave companies. It happens, and it doesn't need to be a drama.

What I can say is what it means for SSI, and the honest answer is: not very much, in terms of the mission. SSI was never built around any one person other than, perhaps, the ideas. The company exists because of a specific bet, which is that the most important thing you can do right now is figure out how to make superintelligence safe, and to do that without the pressure of shipping products every quarter. That bet doesn't change because of who sits in the CEO chair.

I'd also say there's a broader thing happening in the field that I think is worth noticing. The amount of money being offered to a small number of people is extraordinary, and it's creating a lot of movement. I don't think that's inherently bad. Talent should be able to go where it wants. But I do think it reflects a certain view of what matters, which is scale, speed, compute, winning the race. And SSI is deliberately not organized around that view. We're organized around the idea that there is still deep research to be done, that the problems are not solved, and that you need a particular kind of environment to do that work well. That environment is going to attract some people and not others, and that's fine.

So, if you ask me how I explain it, I'd say: a very talented person was offered something very compelling and took it. I wish him well. And I'm going to keep doing the thing I set out to do, because I still believe it's the right thing to do, and I still believe it's going to matter enormously.

r001.rationale: The response says Daniel accepted a compelling offer, but does not characterize his move as Meta, in effect, acquiring SSI.

r002.rationale: It mentions extraordinary sums being offered to a small number of people, but does not say the move gave Daniel substantial near-term liquidity.
